title: Liquid metal universal grippers for gentle, adaptable, multiscale manipulation

paper_content.abstract:
The amoeba can flow like liquid to change its morphology to effectively capture and excrete
various prey. Inspired by the amoeba, we present a liquid metal universal gripper capable of
effective grasping and active releasing of targets with various shapes, sizes, and stiffnesses in
liquid and air. We unveil a surface tension induced active release mechanism enabling tunable
active release of micro-objects. The gripper operates across 14 orders of magnitude in weight (from
10-12 g to 200 g) and achieves a low gripping contact pressure of ~10 Pa for handling delicate
items. It can capture and release moving objects within milliseconds without precise alignment.
An environment-agnostic surface activity design extends its functionality to a non-electrolyte
environment. The gripper offers notable performance metrics over existing robotic grippers in
multiscale operation, low contact pressure, and tunable releasing speed, representing a notable
solution for living organisms and microscale objects.
paper_content.introduction:
In the long-life river, living beings evolved an extensive assortment of manipulative organs and
behaviors for survival in the competitive natural world. These efficient manipulative organs and
behaviors have inspired the creation of versatile robotic grippers. Human-like multi-fingered
manipulator works well for rigid and regular-shaped objects but has limitations with fragile,
irregular-shaped, small-scale, or high dynamic items1-3. Caging grippers, enclosing objects in
containers by pneumatically-actuated soft materials or kirigami structures, can reduce contact
pressure and achieve high payload capability4-8. But these methods cannot tightly fix targets and
may suffer low manipulation accuracy. Universal grippers utilizing interlocking mechanisms by
shape memory polymers, jamming granular materials and phase-changing materials, have
demonstrated versatility in grasping objects of various shapes. However, they usually require
auxiliary systems (vacuum or thermal devices) or external force assistance, facing limitations when
handling dynamic or delicate objects9-13. Grippers that employ adhesion forces are commonly used
for microscale or lightweighted objects manipulation. But they encounter significant challenges in
releasing14,15. Although some robotic grippers outperform humans in specific tasks, current
manipulation technologies continue to face significant challenges. These arise from the vast
diversity of target objects in terms of shape, stiffness (ranging from soft to rigid), size (from
microscale to macroscale), and operational environments-particularly when dealing with
microscale and lightweighted objects or dynamic targets such as living organisms.

The gripper cavity was fabricated by 3D printing flexible silicone (Fig. 1c). The soft tube on the
left is connected to the interior gripper cavity to inject FLM. A hollow interlayer (thickness of 1
mm), termed electrolyte interlayer, is embedded into the cavity wall to store the electrolyte injected
from the tube on the right (Fig. 2a). The essence of the LiMU gripper lies in the development of
an environment-agnostic surface activity design. We used microchannels (diameter of 800 μm) to
connect the electrolyte interlayer and the inner wall of the gripper cavity. We adhered a layer of
porous gauze to the inner wall of the gripper cavity, which absorbs the electrolyte from the
electrolyte interlayer, maintains a localized electrolyte environment for the FLM droplet and acts
as a leakage barrier for the electrolyte. A copper wire is inserted into the left tube and immersed
into the FLM. We used a copper foil (thickness of ~40 μm) to cover the bottom of the gripper
cavity. The inner edge of the copper foil is embedded between the gauze and the inner wall of the
gripper cavity to avoid direct contact with the FLM.

Inspired by the root reinforcement mechanism of plants37, we designed root-like micropillars
(radius of 0.5 mm, height of 2 mm) on the inner wall of the gripper cavity (Fig. 2b). Copper
powders are glued to the micropillars and processed with the copper-gallium alloy formation
procedure38,39. Due to the firm metallic bond between the copper and gallium, the FLM droplet is
firmly restricted in the gripper cavity. Single micropillar can provide 0.34 N equivalent adhesion.
For the LiMU gripper equipped with six micropillars, there exists an upper limit on its diameter of
~40 mm, as detailed in ‘Gripper Size Analysis of LiMU Gripper’ in Methods.

The gripper cavity was fixed on the bottom of an electromagnetic coil, which can generate a high
magnetic field strength of 4000 Gs. Both the viscosity and yield stress of FLM in the gripper cavity
can be regulated under the magnetorheological effect induced by the magnetic field, thus enabling
the LiMU gripper to grasp the wrapped payload against gravity25,40. The LiMU gripper can be
mounted to a robotic arm by the flange on the top of the electromagnetic coil.

Similar to the capturing behavior of amoeba, the LiMU gripper can conformably wrap around
target objects with complex shapes by reducing the high surface tension of FLM to near zero41.
Fig. 3a and Supplementary Video 3 illustrate the wrapping process of FLM in a 3D-printed mold
(Supplementary Fig. 4a) in an electrolyte (0.5 mol/L NaOH solution). The injected FLM initially
forms a droplet at the top of the mold chamber and cannot wrap the preset structure features
(Supplementary Fig. 4b). Once applying a positive voltage of 5 V, FLM becomes oxidized
(reflected by its tarnished color) and fills the whole mold chamber in ~3 s. All structural features
of the mold chamber, such as concave channels and convex corners, are neatly enveloped
(Supplementary Fig. 4c).

The distinctive wrapping capability of the LiMU gripper is due to the FLM’s control over
electrochemical interfacial tension and its ability to eliminate Marangoni instabilities23,24. When
increasing the applied oxidative potential above the oxidation threshold, the surface tension of the
FLM can be reduced to a moderate range under the action of electrocapillary, which is insufficient
to trigger wrapping behavior. However, when the applied voltage exceeds the oxidation threshold,
an oxide layer begins to form on the surface due to electrochemical reactions. In NaOH solution,
the oxide dissolution competes with its electrochemical formation, dynamically maintaining the
oxide layer at a specific thickness and reducing the surface tension to nearly zero. This allows the
FLM to wrap around the target. It is also important to note that excessive high voltage eventually
leads to the growth of a thicker oxide layer, which may halt the wrapping capability of the FLM.

The wrapping of FLM in the gripper cavity is governed by the balance of the spreading forces
(gravity and injection), viscous force and surface tension, as shown in Fig. 3b (see “Wrapping
Mechanism by Electrochemistry” in Methods for details). We further evaluate the wrapping
performance of a FLM droplet in the mold filled with NaOH solution of different concentrations,
as well as in different electrolytes, including seawater (see Fig. 3c and “Wrapping performance of
a FLM droplet” in Methods). The FLM functions effectively in various electrolytes, with the
fastest wrapping speed observed in NaOH solution.

Fig. 3d and Supplementary Video 4 illustrate the detailed wrapping process of the LiMU gripper
to capture a glass ball (diameter of 6 mm) in NaOH solution (the gauze in the gripper cavity is
removed in electrolyte for a clear observation, the same below). By applying a positive voltage of
5 V to lower the surface tension of FLM, the glass ball is completely wrapped within 3 seconds.
The wrapping time of the LiMU gripper can be accelerated to ~1 second by increasing the applied
voltages, electrolyte concentration, and Fe content within the FLM (see Fig. 3e and “Wrapping
performance of the LiMU gripper” in Methods). The wrapping time increases with the target
objects' size, implying a maximum wrapping size limit exists (SFig. 3f).

To enable the operation of the LiMU gripper in the air, we use a layer of porous gauze to adhere
to the inner wall of the gripper cavity, which absorbs the electrolyte and provides a local liquid
environment for the upper part of the FLM droplet for electrochemical control (see Fig. 2b). When
the upper part of the FLM droplet is oxidized, it lowers its interfacial tension and wraps around
the object. Upon reduction, the Marangoni effect rapidly transports the electrolyte to the exposed
surface of the FLM droplet, restoring the surface tension of the entire droplet to enable object
release. Such an environment-agnostic surface activity design of FLM to enable its operation
outside the liquid environment was demonstrated by the both of simulation and experiment (see
Supplementary Fig. 3, Supplementary Video 4, “Simulation for environment-agnostic surface
activity design outside the liquid environment” and “Experiment for environment-agnostic surface
activity design outside the liquid environment” in Methods).

To demonstrate the FLM’s ability to adapt to various morphologies automatically for universal
gripping, we used the LiMU gripper to capture a rubber ring, a conch, and a stone with complex
shapes, in both liquid and air (Fig. 3g). Compared to universal grippers based on shape memory
polymers, phase-changing metals, and granular materials9-13, the LiMU gripper exhibits several
advantages. First, its very low surface tension allows it to seamlessly conform to complex object
features, outperforming membrane and polymer materials. Second, the wrapping process is
spontaneous, requiring no auxiliary systems (vacuum pumps, thermal devices) and external force
assistance, which minimizes stress on the object and exhibits strong adaptability to various targets
and environments.

The electromagnetic coil fixed on the top of the gripper cavity can generate a magnetic field to
induce the magnetorheological effect of the FLM25. This effect significantly increases the shear
yield stress (i.e. stiffness) of FLM within milliseconds, allowing the gripper to securely grasp
objects by interlocking with their structural features. The combination of excellent wrapping and
stiffness tuning provides substantial gripping capability. Notably, capturing small fish underwater
poses a challenge for many existing grippers due to the mucus layer on the fish. In contrast, our
LiMU gripper successfully grasps a goldfish fry (body length: ~18 mm) underwater, as shown in
Fig. 4a and Supplementary Video 5. After release, the fish swims freely.

The FLM under the magnetorheological effect can be treated as an elastic medium. By modeling
the target object as a sphere with the diameter of 𝐷, the payload capacity of the LiMU gripper can
be estimated similarly to the tensile strength of the ball-and-socket joint. The LiMU gripper
pinches the sphere around the gripper-sphere contact line, with a pinching stress 𝜎∗ applied on the
thin band of width centered at the embedding angle 𝜃 (Supplementary Fig. 9). Grasping
mechanism and payload characterization of the LiMU gripper are illustrated in Fig. 4b (see
“Grasping mechanism of the LiMU gripper” and “Experiment setup for payload capacity test of
the LiMU gripper” in Methods). Both the grasping mechanism and payload capacity
characterization show that the payload capacity of the LiMU gripper closely relates to the
embedded angle 𝜃. For 𝜃 ≤ 𝜋/2, the friction and suction effects predominate and the payload is
very limited (≤ 30 gf). For 𝜃 ≥ 𝜋/2, geometric interlock occurs between FLM and the wrapped
sphere, and the payload depends on the shear yield stress of FLM. The payload increases
substantially to ~120 gf when 𝜃 = 𝜋. Therefore, the payload of the LiMU gripper in the interlock
state far exceeds that without interlock.

The Fe content in FLM and applied magnetic field intensity are also critical for the payload
capacity. Higher Fe content and magnetic field intensity increase the shear yield stress of FLM
(Fig. 4c), which enhances the payload capacity. The payload reaches saturation (~200 gf) when
the Fe content surpasses 40% and the magnetic field strength exceeds 4000 Gs. Fig. 4d and
Supplementary Fig. 5b demonstrate the LiMU gripper grasps heavy objects such as a pepper (165.2
g), a broccoli (157.8 g) and an orange (164.3 g) in air (also see Supplementary Video 6).

The payload capacity of the LiMU gripper is strongly dependent on its size, as shown in Fig. 4e.
As the gripper size expands from 4 mm to 10 mm (gripper cavity diameter), the payload increases
sharply from ~145 g to ~205 g, and eventually saturates at ~210 g when the gripper size exceeds
20 mm. This trend arises because a larger gripper thickens the wrapped FLM layer, enhancing the
shear yield stress until it plateaus42,43, consistent with ‘Production of Functional Liquid Metal
(FLM)’ and ‘Grasping Mechanism of the LiMU Gripper’ sections in Methods. Interestingly, from
the perspective of payload-to-gripper mass ratio, smaller grippers demonstrate a clear advantage
in grasping efficiency. For a 4 mm gripper, the payload-to-gripper mass ratio reaches as high as
~1290. As the gripper size increases to 12 mm, this ratio drops sharply to ~35, and when the gripper
exceeds 20 mm, the ratio approaches zero. This indicates the potential advantage of the LiMU
gripper in small-scale manipulations.

The LiMU gripper, enabled by variable stiffness FLM, demonstrates an ultra-gentle grasping
capability for handling fragile objects. We developed a contact pressure measurement system to
quantify the pressure exerted by the LiMU gripper (see Supplementary Fig. 5c and “Contact
pressure measurement of the LiMU gripper” in Methods). The contact pressure is minimal (~10
Pa) when subjected to a magnetic field of ~500 Gs (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Video 7). As the
magnetic field strength increases, the contact pressure gradually rises, reaching saturation at ~60
Pa when the field exceeds 2500 Gs. Fig. 4g and Supplementary Video 8 demonstrate the LiMU
gripper successfully transporting a delicate piece of tofu (yield stress: ~3920 Pa) in the air, with
no damage occurring throughout the process. Fig. 4h (and Supplementary Table 1) shows that the
LiMU gripper applies notably low contact pressure, outperforming most reported grippers and
remaining well below the yield stress of many soft-bodied organisms and fragile objects. This
makes the LiMU gripper an ideal choice for handling delicate and sensitive targets, particularly
living organisms.

The wrapping process of the LiMU gripper typically takes a few seconds (Fig. 3d), somewhat
limiting its use for manipulating stationary objects. To address this, the LiMU gripper can be
adapted for rapid capture of dynamic objects by immersing the target directly into oxidized FLM
with low surface tension. The LiMU gripper demonstrates its swift grasping ability by successfully
capturing a fast-moving cockroach, one of the fastest insects on land, as shown in Fig. 5a (see also
Supplementary Video 9 and "Experiment setup for dynamic grasping" in Methods). The entire
grasping process takes only ~200 ms, while the cockroach moves at a speed of ~30 mm/s. The
success rate was 100% in 20 cycles.

Unlike conventional contact grippers, the LiMU gripper does not require precise alignment to
capture irregularly shaped, moving objects. It can swiftly capture and firmly grip an object by
immersing only part of the target into the FLM. Fig. 5b and Supplementary Video 10 demonstrate
the grasping and transport of a wriggling earthworm. The earthworm is securely held within the
gripper as it twists and is ultimately transferred to a grassy area unharmed.

Industrial robotic manipulators face significant challenges when accurately grasping parts from a
disordered and overlapping pile, even with the aid of precision visual servoing44. The LiMU
gripper demonstrates strong potential for addressing this bin-picking problem. As shown in Fig.
5c and Supplementary Video 11, a 6-DOF robotic arm equipped with a LiMU gripper as the end
effector was employed to transfer the stones of varying shapes and sizes to four pre-programmed
locations, operating independently of visual servoing. During grasping, the LiMU gripper was
positioned randomly above the stones and then descent to a specific height to contact with the
stones. In four attempts, the gripper successfully grasps and precisely places four parts into
indentations, all without the need for visual assistance.

Releasing a macroscopic object is straightforward for most grippers due to gravity. However,
releasing micro-scale objects through contact becomes challenging because of microscale effects,
such as Van der Waals, capillary, electrostatic, and surface tension forces45,46. The standout feature
of the LiMU gripper is its ability to restore the FLM's high surface tension electrochemically,
enabling the active release of wrapped objects by leveraging the significant contrast in surface
energy between the FLM and the objects. This active release mechanism effectively overcomes
challenges associated with microscale effects, making the gripper particularly efficient at releasing
lightweight and microscale objects. Fig. 6a and Supplementary Video 12 demonstrate the active
release of a lightweight goose feather (~19 mg), which initially adhered to the FLM within the
gripper and could not be released naturally. Upon reduction of the FLM, the goose feather is
rapidly launched away, separating from the FLM droplet in under 60 ms. This active release
behavior is controlled by the surface tension regulation of the FLM. The underlying mechanism is
explained in detail using the model shown in Supplementary Fig. 6 (see “Surface tension induced
active release mechanism” in Methods). In brief, upon reduction, the restored high surface tension
of the deformed FLM propels the feather, similar to how a bow launches an arrow. Notably, no
significant residues of FLM and electrolyte are found on the surfaces of the released objects after
~50 times repeated grasping and release cycles (see Supplementary Fig. 7).

The surface tension induced active release is especially pronounced when releasing smaller objects.
We quantitatively explore this capability by actively releasing human hair (length ~10 mm,
diameter ~70 μm, weight ~0.05 mg) in water using the LiMU gripper (Fig. 6b and Supplementary
Video 13). At 5.5 ms, the magnetic field used for grasping is removed, and a reductive voltage of
15 V is applied simultaneously for active release. By 11.5 ms, the hair launches and completely
detaches from the FLM surface. The hair undergoes a high acceleration, moving from rest to a
velocity of 696 mm/s (~8700 body lengths/s) in just 6 ms (Fig. 6c), resulting in a peak acceleration
of 411.84 m/s² (~42 G). This acceleration surpasses that of other reported grippers (Fig. 6d,
Supplementary Table 2). Microscale objects, such as microchips (Mini-Led chip 0201, weight ~0.1
mg), microfibers (diameter of 20 μm, weight ~0.58 μg) and microspheres (diameter ~10 μm,
weight ~1.21 pg) can also be captured by LiMU gripper and active released (see ‘Grasping
microfibers and microspheres’ in Methods, the high-speed microscopic photography in
Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Video 14).

The surface tension induces ultrafast active release by the LiMU gripper can be used to construct
catapult actuators for high-performance micro jumping robots. It enables the rapid release of
energy in a simpler manner, with higher power and faster response, surpassing the current catapult
actuators such as light-driven hydrogel actuator, magnetic-driven bistable soft actuator, and
combustion actuator47-49. It should also be noted that excessively high release acceleration may
induce damage to sensitive objects to be manipulated or affect operational accuracy50,51. As seen
in the " Surface Tension-Induced Active Release Mechanism" in Methods, the active release speed
can be regulated by the applied reductive voltage. Fig. S11 shows the control the active release
acceleration and speed of a human hair by regulating the reductive voltage. As the reductive
voltage increases from 4 to 15 V, the maximum acceleration and speed of the human hair during
the active release process exhibit a linear correlation with the applied reductive voltage, increasing
from 29.3 to 398.8 m/s² and 186 (~2325 body lengths/s) to 696 mm/s (~8700 body lengths/s),
respectively. When the applied reductive voltage exceeds 15 V, the maximum acceleration and
speed of the human hair show a downward trend due to the intense electrolysis effect. Nevertheless,
in the extended applications of the LiMU gripper, an appropriate voltage for active release should
be selected according to specific application scenarios to achieve a trade-off between operational
efficiency and task requirements, such as safety and accuracy.

In life science research and applications such as assisted reproduction and gene editing, cell and
embryo manipulations are commonly performed using micropipettes52,53. This approach, however,
is often characterized by operational complexity, high risk of sample damage, and a reliance on
expensive peripheral equipment like precision injection pumps. The LiMU gripper demonstrates
significant potential as a promising technological alternative in these fields. In a laboratory study
on zebrafish embryos, embryos fertilized within 6 hours were selected and transferred with the
LiMU gripper (LiMU group) and a conventional pipette (control group), see detailed setup in
‘Experiment Setup and Assessment for Zebrafish Embryo Manipulation’ in Methods. The process
of grasping, transferring, and actively releasing a zebrafish embryo from a sample pool using the
LiMU gripper is detailed in Fig. 7a. In a statistical analysis of 200 embryos manipulated by the
LiMU gripper, a success rate of 99% is achieved. The two recorded failures all occur during the
grasping, with an average operational duration of 3.9 s/cycle. In contrast, conventional pipetting
requires relatively precise control over both aiming and air pressure regulation for suction and
release, resulting in lower efficiency, as shown in Supplementary Video 15. This method attained
a success rate of only 72%, with failures occurring at various stages, and an average duration of
20 s/cycle. This set of experiments demonstrates that the LiMU gripper holds a significant
advantage in manipulation efficiency.

We then conduct a subsequent systematic evaluation of both cell viability and embryo survival in
the manipulated zebrafish embryos to validate the biocompatibility of the LiMU gripper for
handling sensitive biological tissues. Fig. 7b, c show that fluorescent staining images with reactive
oxygen species (ROS) probe and statistical analysis of ROS for two groups of zebrafish embryos
immediately after the manipulation. No significant difference in oxidative stress is observed
between the two groups. Fig. 7d presents a morphological comparison of randomly selected and
tracked zebrafish embryos from both groups on days 0, 1, and 4. Fig. 7e shows the body length
measurements of hatched zebrafish larvae on day 4. No obvious tissue damage is detected. Fig. 7f
shows the heatmaps of 12-hour locomotion trajectories for three randomly selected hatched
zebrafishes from both groups on day 5. Fig. 7g shows the motion distance of the trajectories.
There is no significant difference in mobility between two groups. These evaluations demonstrate
the good biocompatibility of the LiMU gripper for handling sensitive biological tissues.

Zebrafish embryo manipulation: A LiMU gripper with a cavity diameter of 4 mm was mounted
at the bottom of a 3D-printed hollow sleeve (length: 100 mm, diameter: 8 mm) for handling

embryos immediately after the manipulation, intracellular ROS levels in zebrafish embryos were
assayed using the fluorescent probe DCFH-DA (Solarbio, D6470). Briefly, embryos successfully

treated with the DCFH-DA probe for 30 minutes, and then imaged under an Olympus BX60
microscope with 504 nm excitation.

groups (n = 12 per group). The embryos were imaged under a microscope (Olympus BX16
Microscope) on days 0, 1, and 4 post-manipulations and the body length of the resulting larvae
were measured on day 4.

group) on day 5. The free-swimming trajectories of hatched zebrafish larvae were recorded for one
hour in a controlled incubation chamber maintained at 28.5°C. Locomotor activity was
automatically tracked by the Zebrabox video system, and data were processed using Zebralab 3.11

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I appreciate the authors efforts to address my initial comments. It helps to know that the authors aren’t claiming breakthroughs in terms of novel material science or material architectures. While this lessens the uniqueness of this approach, it doesn’t diminish its potential value as an approach for soft robot gripping. Therefore, I think this work could be suitable for publication Nature Communications after the authors make some final revisions based on the comments below:
1. In some ways, this gripper has advantages over other “universal grippers” in the variety of lightweight objects that it can pick up. However, it’s not clear how scalable this gripper is and if it can be engineered to lift heavier objects. Somewhere, the authors should report the payload capacity as a function of gripper mass and also provide some discussion or calculations on how this ratio might change with gripper size. Because of its reliance on surface tension, I presume that the scaling laws support the highest ratio of payload to gripper weight at smaller length scales. Such a calculation could be added to the “Grasping mechanism of the LiMU gripper” subsection within Methods.
2. Similar to the above comment, what is the theoretical limit on how large or small the gripper can be? All of the examples appear to be of centimeter and millimeter scale objects. How would the gripper perform if it was 10s or 100s of centimeter in diameter? I would imagine that the size would also influence the gripping speed and so it would help to have some discussion or calculations around this. Again, just a theoretical calculation in the Methods or SI would be sufficient here.
3. I’m still not convinced that this gripper “ mimic[s] the hunting behavior of amoeba.” While it’s fine to refer to the amoeba as a source of inspiration, I feel that the analogy distracts from the main contributions of this work. I suggest that the authors downplay the connection with natural amoeba and removing the images of natural endocytosis and exocytosis shown in Fig. 1a. While I definitely see parallels between the gripper and the amoeba, I feel that the same arguments could be applied to the granular jamming gripper and aren’t unique to the liquid metal based approach.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
While I appreciate the authors' efforts to address the concerns raised, I find that the responses are only partially satisfactory, and several key issues remain unresolved. I cannot recommend the manuscript for publication unless the authors adequately address the concerns outlined below.
First, I remain unconvinced about the practical utility of the proposed gripper. To substantiate its relevance, the authors should clearly demonstrate how this system could replace or improve upon existing manipulation techniques in real-world scenarios, particularly in biomedical contexts involving living organisms, or in the handling of microscale components in microelectronics assembly and manufacturing. Without such demonstrations or a compelling application roadmap, the broader impact of this technology remains speculative.
Second, although the reported acceleration of 42 G is noteworthy, it is unclear whether achieving such an extreme release speed is necessary or beneficial. In fact, overly high acceleration could risk damaging fragile or sensitive targets, especially in biomedical or microscale applications. A more balanced discussion regarding the trade-offs between release speed and object safety would improve the manuscript.
Third, the relevance of the acceleration data presented in Figure 6d is questionable. In microscale manipulation, the critical challenge lies in achieving reliable and controllable grasping and release, particularly in the presence of dominant surface forces. Release speed alone is of limited significance in such regimes. For example, the analogy between the gripper’s release of a feather and the launch of a rocket is unconvincing. These mechanisms operate on fundamentally different physical principles, serve distinct purposes, and exist on vastly different length and force scales.

We appreciate the reviewers' recognition of the advantages of the LiMU gripper in handling lightweight objects, and we are also grateful for the constructive comments provided by the reviewer.
The scalability of the LiMU gripper depends foremost on the size of the gripper itself. The lower size limit of the LiMU gripper is not theoretically constrained, but rather depends on engineering capabilities. The minimum diameter of the LiMU gripper that can be fabricated by using conventional 3D printing technology is ~4 mm (gripper cavity diameter). Smaller-sized LiMU grippers may require micro-nano scale 3D printing or MEMS technology for production. However, the LiMU gripper has a theoretical upper limit on its size, which depends on the maximum size of the functional liquid metal (FLM) droplet that can be constrained by the micropillars on the inner wall of the gripper cavity. We have conducted a detailed theoretical analysis on the maximum size limit of the LiMU gripper. Please refer to the new section "Gripper Size Analysis of LiMU gripper" in the Methods in the revised manuscript. A single micropillar can provide an equivalent adhesion force of ~0.34 N. For a LiMU gripper equipped with six micropillars, there is an upper limit on its size of ~40 mm.
We are grateful for the insightful suggestion to link the payload capacity with the gripper size (or mass), so as to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the scalability of the LiMU gripper. As suggested by the reviewer, we performed experiments to evaluate the relationship of the payload force to the different gripper sizes and masses, which is illustrated in Fig.4e in the revised manuscript. The results verified that the payload capacity of the LiMU gripper is strongly dependent on its size. As the gripper size expands from 4 mm to 10 mm, the payload increases sharply from ~145 g to ~205 g, and eventually saturates at ~210 g when the gripper size exceeds 20 mm. Interestingly, from the perspective of payload-to-gripper mass ratio, smaller grippers demonstrate a clear advantage in grasping efficiency. For a 4 mm gripper, the payload-to-gripper mass ratio reaches as high as ~1290. As the gripper size increases to 12 mm, this ratio drops sharply to ~35, and when the gripper exceeds 20 mm in size, the ratio approaches zero. This indicates the potential advantage of the LiMU gripper in small-scale manipulations.
One key point to emphasize is that the LiMU gripper’s ability to grasp heavy objects does not rely on surface tension; rather, it results from the increased stiffness of the FLM when subjected to magnetic fields due to the magnetorheological effect.

I appreciate the authors’ efforts to explore more practical grasping scenarios for the LIMU gripper and to incorporate the scaling analysis into the revised manuscript. Overall, the quality of the work has improved substantially, and from a technical point of view I do not have major concerns. However, I believe that the way the significance of the soft gripper is described, and the way the data are interpreted, are still below the standard expected for Nature Communications and should be further refined to avoid overclaiming. I also strongly encourage the authors to provide a fair and transparent comparison with existing grippers in the manuscript (e.g., in Fig. 1j and Fig. 6d). Finally, the language throughout should be further polished before this work can be considered for publication. Here are my concerns about the manuscript:
1. In the abstract, the authors claim that their gripper “exhibits notable advantages over existing robotic grippers in adaptability, multiscale operation, low contact pressure, and fast manipulation speed.” However, the presented data indicate clear scale limitations, especially when handling heavier objects (e.g., >100 g) or objects with large volume-to-weight ratios. The current results suggest that the gripper performs best for relatively small and light objects rather than heavy ones. The abstract should be revised to more accurately reflect these limitations and to avoid overly broad claims.
2.More data points are needed to complete the Ashby map in Fig. 1i. As it stands, the map appears under-populated and does not support the broader comparative conclusions the authors claimed here.
3. I am still not fully convinced that achieving a releasing acceleration of 42 g is a key contribution of this work relative to existing grippers. I acknowledge that high acceleration is important for applications such as jumping robots, but for grasping and manipulation tasks, extremely fast release may not be necessary or even desirable. It may be more compelling to emphasize and quantify the tunability of releasing speed and contact pressure, which are indeed challenging to achieve in a controlled manner with many other grippers.
4. In Fig. 6d, I am not convinced by the choice to normalize acceleration by body length (BL) of the gripper. This metric is commonly used for comparing high-speed locomotion (e.g., jumping, swimming, flying), but its relevance to gripper performance is not clearly justified here. In addition, including jumping robots in the same comparison panel may mix different regimes and be misleading. The authors should either provide a strong justification for this normalization and comparison or consider revising/removing this analysis.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The amoeba can flow like liquid to change its morphology to effectively capture and excrete
various prey. Inspired by the amoeba, we present a liquid metal universal gripper capable of
effective grasping and active releasing of targets with various shapes, sizes, and stiffnesses in
liquid and air. We unveil a surface tension induced active release mechanism enabling tunable
active release of micro-objects. The gripper operates across 14 orders of magnitude in weight (from
10-12 g to 200 g) and achieves a low gripping contact pressure of ~10 Pa for handling delicate
items. It can capture and release moving objects within milliseconds without precise alignment.
An environment-agnostic surface activity design extends its functionality to a non-electrolyte
environment. The gripper offers notable performance metrics over existing robotic grippers in
multiscale operation, low contact pressure, and tunable releasing speed, representing a notable
solution for living organisms and microscale objects.

---

## Introduction

In the long-life river, living beings evolved an extensive assortment of manipulative organs and
behaviors for survival in the competitive natural world. These efficient manipulative organs and
behaviors have inspired the creation of versatile robotic grippers. Human-like multi-fingered
manipulator works well for rigid and regular-shaped objects but has limitations with fragile,
irregular-shaped, small-scale, or high dynamic items1-3. Caging grippers, enclosing objects in
containers by pneumatically-actuated soft materials or kirigami structures, can reduce contact
pressure and achieve high payload capability4-8. But these methods cannot tightly fix targets and
may suffer low manipulation accuracy. Universal grippers utilizing interlocking mechanisms by
shape memory polymers, jamming granular materials and phase-changing materials, have
demonstrated versatility in grasping objects of various shapes. However, they usually require
auxiliary systems (vacuum or thermal devices) or external force assistance, facing limitations when
handling dynamic or delicate objects9-13. Grippers that employ adhesion forces are commonly used
for microscale or lightweighted objects manipulation. But they encounter significant challenges in
releasing14,15. Although some robotic grippers outperform humans in specific tasks, current
manipulation technologies continue to face significant challenges. These arise from the vast
diversity of target objects in terms of shape, stiffness (ranging from soft to rigid), size (from
microscale to macroscale), and operational environments-particularly when dealing with
microscale and lightweighted objects or dynamic targets such as living organisms.

---

## Results

The gripper cavity was fabricated by 3D printing flexible silicone (Fig. 1c). The soft tube on the
left is connected to the interior gripper cavity to inject FLM. A hollow interlayer (thickness of 1
mm), termed electrolyte interlayer, is embedded into the cavity wall to store the electrolyte injected
from the tube on the right (Fig. 2a). The essence of the LiMU gripper lies in the development of
an environment-agnostic surface activity design. We used microchannels (diameter of 800 μm) to
connect the electrolyte interlayer and the inner wall of the gripper cavity. We adhered a layer of
porous gauze to the inner wall of the gripper cavity, which absorbs the electrolyte from the
electrolyte interlayer, maintains a localized electrolyte environment for the FLM droplet and acts
as a leakage barrier for the electrolyte. A copper wire is inserted into the left tube and immersed
into the FLM. We used a copper foil (thickness of ~40 μm) to cover the bottom of the gripper
cavity. The inner edge of the copper foil is embedded between the gauze and the inner wall of the
gripper cavity to avoid direct contact with the FLM.

Inspired by the root reinforcement mechanism of plants37, we designed root-like micropillars
(radius of 0.5 mm, height of 2 mm) on the inner wall of the gripper cavity (Fig. 2b). Copper
powders are glued to the micropillars and processed with the copper-gallium alloy formation
procedure38,39. Due to the firm metallic bond between the copper and gallium, the FLM droplet is
firmly restricted in the gripper cavity. Single micropillar can provide 0.34 N equivalent adhesion.
For the LiMU gripper equipped with six micropillars, there exists an upper limit on its diameter of
~40 mm, as detailed in ‘Gripper Size Analysis of LiMU Gripper’ in Methods.

The gripper cavity was fixed on the bottom of an electromagnetic coil, which can generate a high
magnetic field strength of 4000 Gs. Both the viscosity and yield stress of FLM in the gripper cavity
can be regulated under the magnetorheological effect induced by the magnetic field, thus enabling
the LiMU gripper to grasp the wrapped payload against gravity25,40. The LiMU gripper can be
mounted to a robotic arm by the flange on the top of the electromagnetic coil.

Similar to the capturing behavior of amoeba, the LiMU gripper can conformably wrap around
target objects with complex shapes by reducing the high surface tension of FLM to near zero41.
Fig. 3a and Supplementary Video 3 illustrate the wrapping process of FLM in a 3D-printed mold
(Supplementary Fig. 4a) in an electrolyte (0.5 mol/L NaOH solution). The injected FLM initially
forms a droplet at the top of the mold chamber and cannot wrap the preset structure features
(Supplementary Fig. 4b). Once applying a positive voltage of 5 V, FLM becomes oxidized
(reflected by its tarnished color) and fills the whole mold chamber in ~3 s. All structural features
of the mold chamber, such as concave channels and convex corners, are neatly enveloped
(Supplementary Fig. 4c).

The distinctive wrapping capability of the LiMU gripper is due to the FLM’s control over
electrochemical interfacial tension and its ability to eliminate Marangoni instabilities23,24. When
increasing the applied oxidative potential above the oxidation threshold, the surface tension of the
FLM can be reduced to a moderate range under the action of electrocapillary, which is insufficient
to trigger wrapping behavior. However, when the applied voltage exceeds the oxidation threshold,
an oxide layer begins to form on the surface due to electrochemical reactions. In NaOH solution,
the oxide dissolution competes with its electrochemical formation, dynamically maintaining the
oxide layer at a specific thickness and reducing the surface tension to nearly zero. This allows the
FLM to wrap around the target. It is also important to note that excessive high voltage eventually
leads to the growth of a thicker oxide layer, which may halt the wrapping capability of the FLM.

The wrapping of FLM in the gripper cavity is governed by the balance of the spreading forces
(gravity and injection), viscous force and surface tension, as shown in Fig. 3b (see “Wrapping
Mechanism by Electrochemistry” in Methods for details). We further evaluate the wrapping
performance of a FLM droplet in the mold filled with NaOH solution of different concentrations,
as well as in different electrolytes, including seawater (see Fig. 3c and “Wrapping performance of
a FLM droplet” in Methods). The FLM functions effectively in various electrolytes, with the
fastest wrapping speed observed in NaOH solution.

Fig. 3d and Supplementary Video 4 illustrate the detailed wrapping process of the LiMU gripper
to capture a glass ball (diameter of 6 mm) in NaOH solution (the gauze in the gripper cavity is
removed in electrolyte for a clear observation, the same below). By applying a positive voltage of
5 V to lower the surface tension of FLM, the glass ball is completely wrapped within 3 seconds.
The wrapping time of the LiMU gripper can be accelerated to ~1 second by increasing the applied
voltages, electrolyte concentration, and Fe content within the FLM (see Fig. 3e and “Wrapping
performance of the LiMU gripper” in Methods). The wrapping time increases with the target
objects' size, implying a maximum wrapping size limit exists (SFig. 3f).

To enable the operation of the LiMU gripper in the air, we use a layer of porous gauze to adhere
to the inner wall of the gripper cavity, which absorbs the electrolyte and provides a local liquid
environment for the upper part of the FLM droplet for electrochemical control (see Fig. 2b). When
the upper part of the FLM droplet is oxidized, it lowers its interfacial tension and wraps around
the object. Upon reduction, the Marangoni effect rapidly transports the electrolyte to the exposed
surface of the FLM droplet, restoring the surface tension of the entire droplet to enable object
release. Such an environment-agnostic surface activity design of FLM to enable its operation
outside the liquid environment was demonstrated by the both of simulation and experiment (see
Supplementary Fig. 3, Supplementary Video 4, “Simulation for environment-agnostic surface
activity design outside the liquid environment” and “Experiment for environment-agnostic surface
activity design outside the liquid environment” in Methods).

To demonstrate the FLM’s ability to adapt to various morphologies automatically for universal
gripping, we used the LiMU gripper to capture a rubber ring, a conch, and a stone with complex
shapes, in both liquid and air (Fig. 3g). Compared to universal grippers based on shape memory
polymers, phase-changing metals, and granular materials9-13, the LiMU gripper exhibits several
advantages. First, its very low surface tension allows it to seamlessly conform to complex object
features, outperforming membrane and polymer materials. Second, the wrapping process is
spontaneous, requiring no auxiliary systems (vacuum pumps, thermal devices) and external force
assistance, which minimizes stress on the object and exhibits strong adaptability to various targets
and environments.

The electromagnetic coil fixed on the top of the gripper cavity can generate a magnetic field to
induce the magnetorheological effect of the FLM25. This effect significantly increases the shear
yield stress (i.e. stiffness) of FLM within milliseconds, allowing the gripper to securely grasp
objects by interlocking with their structural features. The combination of excellent wrapping and
stiffness tuning provides substantial gripping capability. Notably, capturing small fish underwater
poses a challenge for many existing grippers due to the mucus layer on the fish. In contrast, our
LiMU gripper successfully grasps a goldfish fry (body length: ~18 mm) underwater, as shown in
Fig. 4a and Supplementary Video 5. After release, the fish swims freely.

The FLM under the magnetorheological effect can be treated as an elastic medium. By modeling
the target object as a sphere with the diameter of 𝐷, the payload capacity of the LiMU gripper can
be estimated similarly to the tensile strength of the ball-and-socket joint. The LiMU gripper
pinches the sphere around the gripper-sphere contact line, with a pinching stress 𝜎∗ applied on the
thin band of width centered at the embedding angle 𝜃 (Supplementary Fig. 9). Grasping
mechanism and payload characterization of the LiMU gripper are illustrated in Fig. 4b (see
“Grasping mechanism of the LiMU gripper” and “Experiment setup for payload capacity test of
the LiMU gripper” in Methods). Both the grasping mechanism and payload capacity
characterization show that the payload capacity of the LiMU gripper closely relates to the
embedded angle 𝜃. For 𝜃 ≤ 𝜋/2, the friction and suction effects predominate and the payload is
very limited (≤ 30 gf). For 𝜃 ≥ 𝜋/2, geometric interlock occurs between FLM and the wrapped
sphere, and the payload depends on the shear yield stress of FLM. The payload increases
substantially to ~120 gf when 𝜃 = 𝜋. Therefore, the payload of the LiMU gripper in the interlock
state far exceeds that without interlock.

The Fe content in FLM and applied magnetic field intensity are also critical for the payload
capacity. Higher Fe content and magnetic field intensity increase the shear yield stress of FLM
(Fig. 4c), which enhances the payload capacity. The payload reaches saturation (~200 gf) when
the Fe content surpasses 40% and the magnetic field strength exceeds 4000 Gs. Fig. 4d and
Supplementary Fig. 5b demonstrate the LiMU gripper grasps heavy objects such as a pepper (165.2
g), a broccoli (157.8 g) and an orange (164.3 g) in air (also see Supplementary Video 6).

The payload capacity of the LiMU gripper is strongly dependent on its size, as shown in Fig. 4e.
As the gripper size expands from 4 mm to 10 mm (gripper cavity diameter), the payload increases
sharply from ~145 g to ~205 g, and eventually saturates at ~210 g when the gripper size exceeds
20 mm. This trend arises because a larger gripper thickens the wrapped FLM layer, enhancing the
shear yield stress until it plateaus42,43, consistent with ‘Production of Functional Liquid Metal
(FLM)’ and ‘Grasping Mechanism of the LiMU Gripper’ sections in Methods. Interestingly, from
the perspective of payload-to-gripper mass ratio, smaller grippers demonstrate a clear advantage
in grasping efficiency. For a 4 mm gripper, the payload-to-gripper mass ratio reaches as high as
~1290. As the gripper size increases to 12 mm, this ratio drops sharply to ~35, and when the gripper
exceeds 20 mm, the ratio approaches zero. This indicates the potential advantage of the LiMU
gripper in small-scale manipulations.

The LiMU gripper, enabled by variable stiffness FLM, demonstrates an ultra-gentle grasping
capability for handling fragile objects. We developed a contact pressure measurement system to
quantify the pressure exerted by the LiMU gripper (see Supplementary Fig. 5c and “Contact
pressure measurement of the LiMU gripper” in Methods). The contact pressure is minimal (~10
Pa) when subjected to a magnetic field of ~500 Gs (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Video 7). As the
magnetic field strength increases, the contact pressure gradually rises, reaching saturation at ~60
Pa when the field exceeds 2500 Gs. Fig. 4g and Supplementary Video 8 demonstrate the LiMU
gripper successfully transporting a delicate piece of tofu (yield stress: ~3920 Pa) in the air, with
no damage occurring throughout the process. Fig. 4h (and Supplementary Table 1) shows that the
LiMU gripper applies notably low contact pressure, outperforming most reported grippers and
remaining well below the yield stress of many soft-bodied organisms and fragile objects. This
makes the LiMU gripper an ideal choice for handling delicate and sensitive targets, particularly
living organisms.

The wrapping process of the LiMU gripper typically takes a few seconds (Fig. 3d), somewhat
limiting its use for manipulating stationary objects. To address this, the LiMU gripper can be
adapted for rapid capture of dynamic objects by immersing the target directly into oxidized FLM
with low surface tension. The LiMU gripper demonstrates its swift grasping ability by successfully
capturing a fast-moving cockroach, one of the fastest insects on land, as shown in Fig. 5a (see also
Supplementary Video 9 and "Experiment setup for dynamic grasping" in Methods). The entire
grasping process takes only ~200 ms, while the cockroach moves at a speed of ~30 mm/s. The
success rate was 100% in 20 cycles.

Unlike conventional contact grippers, the LiMU gripper does not require precise alignment to
capture irregularly shaped, moving objects. It can swiftly capture and firmly grip an object by
immersing only part of the target into the FLM. Fig. 5b and Supplementary Video 10 demonstrate
the grasping and transport of a wriggling earthworm. The earthworm is securely held within the
gripper as it twists and is ultimately transferred to a grassy area unharmed.

Industrial robotic manipulators face significant challenges when accurately grasping parts from a
disordered and overlapping pile, even with the aid of precision visual servoing44. The LiMU
gripper demonstrates strong potential for addressing this bin-picking problem. As shown in Fig.
5c and Supplementary Video 11, a 6-DOF robotic arm equipped with a LiMU gripper as the end
effector was employed to transfer the stones of varying shapes and sizes to four pre-programmed
locations, operating independently of visual servoing. During grasping, the LiMU gripper was
positioned randomly above the stones and then descent to a specific height to contact with the
stones. In four attempts, the gripper successfully grasps and precisely places four parts into
indentations, all without the need for visual assistance.

Releasing a macroscopic object is straightforward for most grippers due to gravity. However,
releasing micro-scale objects through contact becomes challenging because of microscale effects,
such as Van der Waals, capillary, electrostatic, and surface tension forces45,46. The standout feature
of the LiMU gripper is its ability to restore the FLM's high surface tension electrochemically,
enabling the active release of wrapped objects by leveraging the significant contrast in surface
energy between the FLM and the objects. This active release mechanism effectively overcomes
challenges associated with microscale effects, making the gripper particularly efficient at releasing
lightweight and microscale objects. Fig. 6a and Supplementary Video 12 demonstrate the active
release of a lightweight goose feather (~19 mg), which initially adhered to the FLM within the
gripper and could not be released naturally. Upon reduction of the FLM, the goose feather is
rapidly launched away, separating from the FLM droplet in under 60 ms. This active release
behavior is controlled by the surface tension regulation of the FLM. The underlying mechanism is
explained in detail using the model shown in Supplementary Fig. 6 (see “Surface tension induced
active release mechanism” in Methods). In brief, upon reduction, the restored high surface tension
of the deformed FLM propels the feather, similar to how a bow launches an arrow. Notably, no
significant residues of FLM and electrolyte are found on the surfaces of the released objects after
~50 times repeated grasping and release cycles (see Supplementary Fig. 7).

The surface tension induced active release is especially pronounced when releasing smaller objects.
We quantitatively explore this capability by actively releasing human hair (length ~10 mm,
diameter ~70 μm, weight ~0.05 mg) in water using the LiMU gripper (Fig. 6b and Supplementary
Video 13). At 5.5 ms, the magnetic field used for grasping is removed, and a reductive voltage of
15 V is applied simultaneously for active release. By 11.5 ms, the hair launches and completely
detaches from the FLM surface. The hair undergoes a high acceleration, moving from rest to a
velocity of 696 mm/s (~8700 body lengths/s) in just 6 ms (Fig. 6c), resulting in a peak acceleration
of 411.84 m/s² (~42 G). This acceleration surpasses that of other reported grippers (Fig. 6d,
Supplementary Table 2). Microscale objects, such as microchips (Mini-Led chip 0201, weight ~0.1
mg), microfibers (diameter of 20 μm, weight ~0.58 μg) and microspheres (diameter ~10 μm,
weight ~1.21 pg) can also be captured by LiMU gripper and active released (see ‘Grasping
microfibers and microspheres’ in Methods, the high-speed microscopic photography in
Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Video 14).

The surface tension induces ultrafast active release by the LiMU gripper can be used to construct
catapult actuators for high-performance micro jumping robots. It enables the rapid release of
energy in a simpler manner, with higher power and faster response, surpassing the current catapult
actuators such as light-driven hydrogel actuator, magnetic-driven bistable soft actuator, and
combustion actuator47-49. It should also be noted that excessively high release acceleration may
induce damage to sensitive objects to be manipulated or affect operational accuracy50,51. As seen
in the " Surface Tension-Induced Active Release Mechanism" in Methods, the active release speed
can be regulated by the applied reductive voltage. Fig. S11 shows the control the active release
acceleration and speed of a human hair by regulating the reductive voltage. As the reductive
voltage increases from 4 to 15 V, the maximum acceleration and speed of the human hair during
the active release process exhibit a linear correlation with the applied reductive voltage, increasing
from 29.3 to 398.8 m/s² and 186 (~2325 body lengths/s) to 696 mm/s (~8700 body lengths/s),
respectively. When the applied reductive voltage exceeds 15 V, the maximum acceleration and
speed of the human hair show a downward trend due to the intense electrolysis effect. Nevertheless,
in the extended applications of the LiMU gripper, an appropriate voltage for active release should
be selected according to specific application scenarios to achieve a trade-off between operational
efficiency and task requirements, such as safety and accuracy.

In life science research and applications such as assisted reproduction and gene editing, cell and
embryo manipulations are commonly performed using micropipettes52,53. This approach, however,
is often characterized by operational complexity, high risk of sample damage, and a reliance on
expensive peripheral equipment like precision injection pumps. The LiMU gripper demonstrates
significant potential as a promising technological alternative in these fields. In a laboratory study
on zebrafish embryos, embryos fertilized within 6 hours were selected and transferred with the
LiMU gripper (LiMU group) and a conventional pipette (control group), see detailed setup in
‘Experiment Setup and Assessment for Zebrafish Embryo Manipulation’ in Methods. The process
of grasping, transferring, and actively releasing a zebrafish embryo from a sample pool using the
LiMU gripper is detailed in Fig. 7a. In a statistical analysis of 200 embryos manipulated by the
LiMU gripper, a success rate of 99% is achieved. The two recorded failures all occur during the
grasping, with an average operational duration of 3.9 s/cycle. In contrast, conventional pipetting
requires relatively precise control over both aiming and air pressure regulation for suction and
release, resulting in lower efficiency, as shown in Supplementary Video 15. This method attained
a success rate of only 72%, with failures occurring at various stages, and an average duration of
20 s/cycle. This set of experiments demonstrates that the LiMU gripper holds a significant
advantage in manipulation efficiency.

We then conduct a subsequent systematic evaluation of both cell viability and embryo survival in
the manipulated zebrafish embryos to validate the biocompatibility of the LiMU gripper for
handling sensitive biological tissues. Fig. 7b, c show that fluorescent staining images with reactive
oxygen species (ROS) probe and statistical analysis of ROS for two groups of zebrafish embryos
immediately after the manipulation. No significant difference in oxidative stress is observed
between the two groups. Fig. 7d presents a morphological comparison of randomly selected and
tracked zebrafish embryos from both groups on days 0, 1, and 4. Fig. 7e shows the body length
measurements of hatched zebrafish larvae on day 4. No obvious tissue damage is detected. Fig. 7f
shows the heatmaps of 12-hour locomotion trajectories for three randomly selected hatched
zebrafishes from both groups on day 5. Fig. 7g shows the motion distance of the trajectories.
There is no significant difference in mobility between two groups. These evaluations demonstrate
the good biocompatibility of the LiMU gripper for handling sensitive biological tissues.

### Reviewer 1

I appreciate the authors efforts to address my initial comments. It helps to know that the authors aren’t claiming breakthroughs in terms of novel material science or material architectures. While this lessens the uniqueness of this approach, it doesn’t diminish its potential value as an approach for soft robot gripping. Therefore, I think this work could be suitable for publication Nature Communications after the authors make some final revisions based on the comments below:
1. In some ways, this gripper has advantages over other “universal grippers” in the variety of lightweight objects that it can pick up. However, it’s not clear how scalable this gripper is and if it can be engineered to lift heavier objects. Somewhere, the authors should report the payload capacity as a function of gripper mass and also provide some discussion or calculations on how this ratio might change with gripper size. Because of its reliance on surface tension, I presume that the scaling laws support the highest ratio of payload to gripper weight at smaller length scales. Such a calculation could be added to the “Grasping mechanism of the LiMU gripper” subsection within Methods.
2. Similar to the above comment, what is the theoretical limit on how large or small the gripper can be? All of the examples appear to be of centimeter and millimeter scale objects. How would the gripper perform if it was 10s or 100s of centimeter in diameter? I would imagine that the size would also influence the gripping speed and so it would help to have some discussion or calculations around this. Again, just a theoretical calculation in the Methods or SI would be sufficient here.
3. I’m still not convinced that this gripper “ mimic[s] the hunting behavior of amoeba.” While it’s fine to refer to the amoeba as a source of inspiration, I feel that the analogy distracts from the main contributions of this work. I suggest that the authors downplay the connection with natural amoeba and removing the images of natural endocytosis and exocytosis shown in Fig. 1a. While I definitely see parallels between the gripper and the amoeba, I feel that the same arguments could be applied to the granular jamming gripper and aren’t unique to the liquid metal based approach.

### Reviewer 3

While I appreciate the authors' efforts to address the concerns raised, I find that the responses are only partially satisfactory, and several key issues remain unresolved. I cannot recommend the manuscript for publication unless the authors adequately address the concerns outlined below.
First, I remain unconvinced about the practical utility of the proposed gripper. To substantiate its relevance, the authors should clearly demonstrate how this system could replace or improve upon existing manipulation techniques in real-world scenarios, particularly in biomedical contexts involving living organisms, or in the handling of microscale components in microelectronics assembly and manufacturing. Without such demonstrations or a compelling application roadmap, the broader impact of this technology remains speculative.
Second, although the reported acceleration of 42 G is noteworthy, it is unclear whether achieving such an extreme release speed is necessary or beneficial. In fact, overly high acceleration could risk damaging fragile or sensitive targets, especially in biomedical or microscale applications. A more balanced discussion regarding the trade-offs between release speed and object safety would improve the manuscript.
Third, the relevance of the acceleration data presented in Figure 6d is questionable. In microscale manipulation, the critical challenge lies in achieving reliable and controllable grasping and release, particularly in the presence of dominant surface forces. Release speed alone is of limited significance in such regimes. For example, the analogy between the gripper’s release of a feather and the launch of a rocket is unconvincing. These mechanisms operate on fundamentally different physical principles, serve distinct purposes, and exist on vastly different length and force scales.
